python_igraph.notes: Rust port matches python-igraph within noise on ring-of-cliques (218 µs vs 206 µs) and is ~21% faster on karate (1757 µs vs 2228 µs). On tiny cells (path-10, two-K4-bridge) python-igraph is faster because its per-call Python overhead amortises over a C inner loop that uses bucket-queue Dijkstra — our BinaryHeap version pays log(|V|) per push. Tiny-cell gap will close once we add a bucket-queue specialisation for integer-spaced weights.

notes: Hot loop is the Brandes-Dijkstra weighted edge-betweenness pass, executed once per edge removed (m iterations total). Per iteration is O(|V| * (|E_active| + |V| log |V|)).

Scratch buffers (sigma, dist, visited, pred, stack, delta_v, eb_now, BinaryHeap) are allocated once outside the removal loop and reused; per-iteration cost is dominated by heap pushes / pops, not allocation.
Frontier uses f64::total_cmp ordering after rejecting NaN / negative weights up front, keeping the heap deterministic without an Ord-impl footgun.

Unit weights through this entrypoint reproduce the unweighted CO-006 dendrogram bit-for-bit: enforced by the `unit_weights_match_unweighted_*` integration tests and by 2 proptests (membership/k/dendrogram + repeated-call determinism).

Slowdown vs. CO-006 (~2.6x on karate) is the unavoidable Dijkstra-vs-BFS overhead: BinaryHeap push/pop replaces the O(1) queue ops, and edges that would terminate early in BFS keep re-entering the heap until visited.
